hero.title: Everything a community needs, in one calm workspace
hero.lead: Origin is a social collaboration network built around eight core objects: profiles, ideas, communities, communication, feed, projects, companies, and opportunities. Whether you're starting something new or growing an existing company, your relationships live in one place instead of ten separate tools.

profiles.body: A profile works like a living resume: it carries your experience, skills, and ideas — plus your reputation and relationships — across every community and project you join.

ideas.body: Ideas are the starting point of everything on Origin. Post an idea page for any idea — a small business, an AI startup, a book club, a 10k run — and the people who want to build it find you.

communities.body: Groups around interests, industries, and goals — Startup Founders, Small Businesses, Book Clubs, Community Organizations, Anyone with an Idea — where members find each other.

communication.body: Every community comes with a Matrix room: real-time chat, direct messages, and group discussions over the open Matrix protocol, end-to-end encrypted by default.

feed.body: The feed shows posts, updates, and opportunities from the people and communities you follow. It is a calm stream of what matters in your network, not an engagement machine.

projects.body: Collaborative efforts where community members work together and turn conversations into outcomes.

companies.body: Ventures formed by members inside the network, with team management and opportunity sharing built in.

opportunities.body: Jobs, partnerships, and investments discovered through the social graph — the network surfaces the right opportunities at the right time.

features.sectionComparison: Why Origin instead of ten tools
features.comparisonIntro: Most platforms solve only one part of collaboration. Origin combines them around the social graph — the relationships between members — so nothing gets lost between tools.

slack.gap: but is built for a single workspace — it does not carry profiles, communities, projects, and opportunities across the people you already know.

discord.gap: but is not organized around profiles, communities, projects, and opportunities on a shared social graph.

whatsapp.gap: but is a private chat app — it does not give communities durable profiles, projects, and discovery on a shared social graph.

linkedin.gap: but does not power the communities, chat, and projects that turn connections into collaboration.

meetup.gap: but is built around one-time RSVPs — it does not carry the community, projects, and relationships that grow after the event.

eventbrite.gap: but manages events, not communities — it does not give your group a lasting home with profiles, projects, and opportunities.

notion.gap: but is a document tool — it does not connect the people behind the pages into a community that works together.

asana.gap: but is built for tasks, not relationships — it does not surface the people and communities that make projects happen.

patreon.gap: but is built around subscriptions — it does not give your members profiles, projects, and communities on a shared social graph.

facebook.gap: but is built around an advertising feed — it does not give communities a calm workspace with profiles, projects, and opportunities.

q1.question: How is JoinOrigin different from Discord?
q1.answer: Discord is a chat app. Origin is a social collaboration network — profiles, ideas, communities, chat, feed, projects, and companies all live on one social graph.

q2.question: Is JoinOrigin open source?
q2.answer: The code is open under AGPL-3.0, and communication runs on the open Matrix protocol. Your data stays portable.

q3.question: What is the social graph?
q3.answer: The social graph is the web of relationships between members. Origin is organized around it, so every profile, community, and project connects through people.

q4.question: When will projects and companies launch?
q4.answer: They develop naturally. As people post ideas, visions, and work, they find the people who want to build with them — and projects and companies grow out of those connections instead of waiting for a launch date.

q1.question: What communities can I join?
q1.answer: Anyone can start or join a community around any idea — a small business, an AI startup, helping the homeless, a 10k run, a political movement, a pee-wee league. If it matters to you, it has a place on Origin.

q2.question: Can I start my own community?
q2.answer: Yes. Every member can create a community around any idea and invite the people they want to build with — whether it is a business, a book club, or a run club.

q3.question: Is my data mine?
q3.answer: Yes. You own your identity and your data. Your data is portable and your network graph persists on the open Matrix protocol.

q4.question: How do I find my people?
q4.answer: Browse communities by interest, industry, or goal — from small businesses and book clubs to AI startups and run clubs — then join the ones that match what you want to build. Or start your own for any idea.

q5.question: Can I join anonymously or by name?
q5.answer: You choose. You can participate with a named account or stay anonymous, and communities, rooms, and idea pages can be open to everyone or gated by organizers. These options roll out over time.

hero.title: JoinOrigin docs
hero.lead: Origin is the product: a social collaboration network and community OS. JoinOrigin is the brand and the network behind it. These docs explain the core objects, the roadmap, and the architecture.

profiles.body: Profiles are the portable identity of every member — like a living resume. They carry experience, skills, ideas, reputation, and relationships across every community and project, so who you are travels with you.

communities.body: Communities are groups of people who share interests, industries, goals, and opportunities — around any idea. They are the center of engagement on Origin and the way members find each other.

ideas.body: Every idea gets a home. Post an idea page for anything — a small business, an AI startup, helping the homeless, a 10k run, a book club, a pee-wee league — and find the people who want to build it with you.

communication.body: Communication happens in a Matrix room — real-time chat, direct messages, and group discussions. It runs on the open Matrix protocol, so conversations are portable and can be end-to-end encrypted.

feed.body: Posts, updates, and opportunities from the people and communities you follow — a calm stream of what matters in your network.

projects.body: Projects are collaborative efforts where members work together toward a shared outcome. They connect the social graph to real work inside and across communities.

companies.body: Companies are ventures formed by members of the network. They bring team management and opportunity sharing into the same workspace where the relationships live.

opportunities.body: Opportunities are jobs, partnerships, and investments surfaced through the social graph. The network matches the right opportunity to the right person at the right time.

phase1.body: Profiles, communities, chat, and the social graph. Success metric: members forming durable communities.

phase2.body: Projects, shared workspaces, and tools that turn conversations into joint work. Success metric: communities shipping outcomes together.

phase3.body: Companies and ventures formed by members, with team management and governance. Success metric: companies founded inside the network.

phase4.body: AI workers that help communities coordinate, summarize, and match opportunities. Success metric: members collaborating with AI as equals.

phase5.body: Open standards and portability so the network connects across platforms. Success metric: a portable, interoperable social graph.

docs.architectureParagraph1: The social graph is the product: every object hangs off the network of people and their relationships. Communication uses the open Matrix protocol (decentralized, E2EE), and your network graph and connections persist forever, so your relationships stay portable.
docs.architectureParagraph2: Origin is built with React, TypeScript, and Next.js on the web, and NestJS, PostgreSQL, Redis, and Docker in the backend. What stays open is the protocol (Matrix), your data, and the source code under AGPL-3.0.

q1.question: What is JoinOrigin built on?
q1.answer: React, TypeScript, and Next.js on the web; NestJS, PostgreSQL, Redis, and Docker in the backend. Communication runs on the open Matrix protocol.

q2.question: What is Matrix?
q2.answer: Matrix is an open, decentralized communication protocol with end-to-end encryption. Origin runs on it, so conversations — and the network graph behind them — are portable and persist forever.

q4.question: What is live now?
q4.answer: The Community Foundation (Phase 1) is live: profiles, communities, chat, and the social graph are already in use by 2,400+ builders.

privacy.useBody: We use the information we collect to operate the site, manage your account and communities, and improve the product. We do not sell your personal information.
privacy.identityBody: You choose how you show up on Origin. glossary.title: Community OS Glossary
glossary.intro: The essential vocabulary of community building — clear definitions for the terms organizers, moderators, and founders use every day.
glossary.whyBody: Community building has its own language, and the terms are often used loosely. A community OS glossary gives organizers, moderators, and founders shared definitions they can rely on — from the classic concepts like moderation and onboarding to newer ideas like engagement loops and hybrid events.
glossary.termsIntro: Here are the core terms every organizer, moderator, and founder uses — each one is defined in practice across the Community Building guides:
glossary.goDeeperItem1: Work through the <1>Community Building guides</1> — the step-by-step how-tos behind every term.
glossary.goDeeperItem2: See the concepts in practice: <1>New York City</1> and <2>Berlin</2> city pages.

community.name: Community
community.definition: A group of people who share interests, industries, goals, or opportunities and connect around them. On Origin, every community comes with a room where members find each other and build together.

community-manager.name: Community manager
community-manager.definition: The person who keeps a community welcoming, active, and on-mission — welcoming new members, sparking conversation, and coordinating projects. On Origin, the member who starts a community owns and moderates its room.

community-os.name: Community OS
community-os.definition: A platform that brings profiles, communities, chat, projects, and opportunities into one organized workspace. Origin is the community OS behind JoinOrigin.

moderation.name: Moderation
moderation.definition: The practice of keeping a community safe and on-topic through clear guidelines and consistent, fair enforcement. Good moderation protects the relationships that make a community worth joining.

onboarding.name: Onboarding
onboarding.definition: The process of welcoming new members and helping them take a first meaningful action — introducing themselves, joining a conversation, or starting a project. Strong onboarding turns new members into active ones.

activation.name: Activation
activation.definition: The moment a new member takes the action that makes them part of the community — their first post, first event, or first project. Activation is the step between joining and contributing.

engagement-loop.name: Engagement loop
engagement-loop.definition: The repeating cycle of participation that keeps a community alive: someone posts, others respond, and the conversation creates more reasons to return. Healthy loops are the heartbeat of an active community.

hybrid-events.name: Hybrid events
hybrid-events.definition: Events that blend in-person and online participation, so members in different places can join the same gathering. Hybrid formats help communities stay connected between meetups.

co-founder.name: Co-founder
co-founder.definition: A person who builds a project or company with you and shares the founding journey. On Origin, co-founders are often found through the network — people who join your idea page and decide to build together.
